title: Fret not (Psalm 37)
hook: don't fret because of evildoers; delight in the Lord
carry: the meek shall inherit the earth

segments.voice: Yesterday, Psalm thirty-four: taste first, then see. Your line was near the brokenhearted, not the strong. Did you eat one bite slowly? Day four hundred twenty-one.

The coworker who cuts corners gets the promotion. The neighbor who never returns anything just bought a boat. The person who was cruel to you in school seems to be thriving, at least online. Say you've done things the honest way, and it hasn't paid off, and they've done it the other way, and it has. It's easy to stew. To replay it in the shower. To check their profile one more time, and come away worse. There's a whole psalm for that. And it opens with two words that sound old-fashioned, but describe that feeling exactly.
screen: `THE CORNER-CUTTER GETS PROMOTED.` → `STEWING IN THE SHOWER.` → `TWO OLD-FASHIONED WORDS.`

segments.voice: Psalm thirty-seven, in the King James Bible: "Fret not thyself because of evildoers, neither be thou envious against the workers of iniquity." Fret, in Hebrew, is linked to a word for burning, getting heated, and verse eight sets it right beside anger and wrath. Don't heat yourself up. Notice the word thyself. Fretting is something you do to you. The person who cheated is out on their boat, and you're the one who's burning. The psalm says they're like grass, which withers quickly. Their success, the psalm says, is real, but it's short. Then instead of fretting, three verbs. Trust: trust in the LORD, and do good. Delight: "Delight thyself also in the LORD; and he shall give thee the desires of thine heart." Not, you'll get whatever you want. More like, delight in God, and your desires themselves begin to change. And rest: "Rest in the LORD, and wait patiently for him: fret not thyself because of him who prospereth in his way." Fret not appears three times in the first eight verses, as if the writer knows you'll need to hear it more than once. Then verse eleven: "But the meek shall inherit the earth; and shall delight themselves in the abundance of peace." Jesus echoes it in the Sermon on the Mount: blessed are the meek. Later, an old man speaks: "I have been young, and now am old." It's a wisdom psalm, more like advice from a grandparent than a prayer. Not everyone's experience matches every line, and the Bible itself has other books, like Job, that wrestle with when the righteous do suffer. But this psalm's counsel is steady: don't let someone else's wrongdoing set you on fire.
screen: `FRET: DON'T HEAT YOURSELF UP.` · `TRUST, DELIGHT, REST.` · `THE MEEK SHALL INHERIT THE EARTH.` · `I HAVE BEEN YOUNG, AND NOW AM OLD.` · then, large: `FRET NOT THYSELF BECAUSE OF EVILDOERS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let go of one grudge. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone whose success, or whose getting away with something, keeps you heated. Notice where the heat sits in your body: jaw, chest, stomach. You don't have to pretend they were right. You don't have to stop wanting justice. Just notice that you're the one burning. On each out-breath, let a little of the heat go. Trust. Delight. Rest. If you pray, you can hand the person, and the justice, to God. If not, simply set the grudge down for this minute. The bell holds the time.
Fret not. Psalm thirty-seven's advice when the wrong people seem to win: don't heat yourself up. Trust, delight, and rest instead.
Your line: the meek shall inherit the earth. Today, the next time you start replaying what someone else got away with, stop, and let that line come to mind instead. Day four hundred twenty-one.

howItsDone: Some Christians turn to Psalm 37 when struggling with envy or injustice, and its line 'the meek shall inherit the earth' is read alongside the Beatitudes in Matthew 5.

fork.setup: the person who cheated is thriving, and you did everything right. what does Psalm 37 tell you to do?
options: fret not: trust, delight, and rest in the LORD.
fork.reveal: fret not thyself, three times in eight verses. instead: trust in the LORD, delight in him, rest and wait patiently.

original.note: Hebrew: fret not, from a root meaning to burn or be heated.

trapdoor: what you thought: don't worry about it.
what it means: don't set yourself on fire over someone else's wrongdoing. trust, delight and rest instead.
what a scholar hears: titchar, linked to charah, to burn; verse 8 pairing it with anger and wrath; and 37:11 behind Jesus' 'blessed are the meek'.

notes: Editor review (y2 days 407–424): hook no longer tells the listener what they did and feel ("You've done things... you stew... feel worse"), now framed as "say"; root-of-fret claim now anchored to verse 8, which sets fret beside anger and wrath; cut stock "a line people sometimes don't realize is from the Psalms"; 37:25 placed correctly (mid-psalm, not "near the end"); "many read" softened in the myth; trapdoor drops the uncited acrostic claim; howItsDone "often" removed.
'Fret' (titchar) from charah, 'to burn, be kindled': standard lexicon. Confirm.
'Fret not' three times in verses 1, 7 and 8; confirm.
The reading of 37:4 (desires reshaped by delight) is one interpretation; phrased as 'more like' and 'many read'. Confirm.
37:25 continues 'yet have I not seen the righteous forsaken, nor his seed begging bread', which can wound; the script quotes only the first clause and acknowledges Job. Confirm.
